title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
1 Learning Objectives
By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

Explain the spatial scan statistic and its underlying logic
Describe the key input files required by SaTScan software
Configure and run a purely spatial Poisson scan in the SaTScan GUI
Reproduce an equivalent analysis in R using SpatialEpi and rsatscan
Correctly interpret output—clusters, relative risk, LLR, and p-values
Recognize the limitations of circular scan statistics

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
2 The Central Question


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
set.seed(42)

# Panel A: random scatter
df_random <- data.frame(
  x = runif(80), y = runif(80), type = "Random"
)

# Panel B: clustered points
centers <- data.frame(cx = c(0.25, 0.72), cy = c(0.3, 0.7))
df_cluster <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:nrow(centers), function(i) {
  n <- if (i == 1) 30 else 10
  data.frame(
    x = rnorm(n, centers$cx[i], 0.07),
    y = rnorm(n, centers$cy[i], 0.07),
    type = "Clustered"
  )
}))
df_cluster <- rbind(df_cluster,
  data.frame(x = runif(40), y = runif(40), type = "Clustered"))

theme_map <- theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_line(color = "grey92"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1A3A5C", size = 12))

p1 <- ggplot(df_random, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(color = "#4A5568", alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  labs(title = "A  Random variation", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  coord_fixed() + theme_map

p2 <- ggplot(df_cluster, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(color = "#1B7A8A", alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  annotate("path",
    x = centers$cx[1] + 0.12 * cos(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out=100)),
    y = centers$cy[1] + 0.12 * sin(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out=100)),
    color = "#F0A500", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "B  Spatial cluster", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  coord_fixed() + theme_map

p1 + p2





Random variation vs. genuine spatial cluster




Disease cases always show some spatial variation. The question is: is the observed concentration beyond what we’d expect by chance? SaTScan answers this with a formal statistical test.

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
3 What Is SaTScan?
SaTScan (developed by Martin Kulldorff, Harvard) is free software that implements the spatial scan statistic—a likelihood ratio test applied to a moving circular window that scans across a study region.






Note



Key facts: Free download at satscan.org. Available since 1997. Widely used by CDC, state health departments, and in academic research.



3.1 Scan types available







Scan Type
Use Case




Purely Spatial
Identify geographic clusters; time ignored


Purely Temporal
Identify time periods with excess cases; space ignored


Space-Time
Clusters elevated in both space and time (outbreaks)


Prospective Spatial
Real-time surveillance at the current date


Spatial Variation in Temporal Trends
Areas where trends diverge from regional average





3.2 Probability models








Model
Data Needed
When to Use




Poisson
Case counts + population
Most public health applications


Bernoulli
Individual case/control indicator
Case-control studies


Space-Time Permutation
Case counts only (no population)
Rapid outbreak investigation


Normal
Continuous outcome
Environmental exposures, income


Multinomial
Multiple disease categories
Comparative disease mapping

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
4 The Spatial Scan Statistic

4.1 Scanning window logic


Code
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(123)

# Simulate a grid of census tracts and case locations
tracts <- expand.grid(x = 1:8, y = 1:6)
tracts$cases <- rpois(nrow(tracts), lambda = 3)
tracts$pop   <- round(runif(nrow(tracts), 800, 2500))

# Inflate cases in a "cluster" region
cluster_mask <- sqrt((tracts$x - 3)^2 + (tracts$y - 4)^2) < 1.8
tracts$cases[cluster_mask] <- tracts$cases[cluster_mask] + rpois(sum(cluster_mask), 12)

# Plot
circle_df <- data.frame(
  x = 3 + 1.8 * cos(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 200)),
  y = 4 + 1.8 * sin(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 200))
)

ggplot(tracts, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = cases / pop * 1000), color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_path(data = circle_df, aes(x, y),
            color = "#F0A500", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = 4, label = "Z\n(scanning\nwindow)",
           color = "#F0A500", size = 3.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#EDF8FB", high = "#1A3A5C",
                      name = "Cases\nper 1,000") +
  labs(title = "SaTScan Scanning Window",
       subtitle = "Window Z moves across every grid cell; radius varies from near-zero to max population %",
       x = "Easting", y = "Northing") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1A3A5C"))





SaTScan imposes circular windows of varying radius at every location, testing each for excess cases.






4.2 The likelihood ratio test
For each window Z, SaTScan computes the log-likelihood ratio (LLR):
\[
\text{LLR}(Z) = \log \left[ \left(\frac{c_Z}{E_Z}\right)^{c_Z} \cdot \left(\frac{C - c_Z}{C - E_Z}\right)^{C - c_Z} \right]
\quad \text{if } c_Z > E_Z, \text{ else } 0
\]
where:

\(c_Z\) = observed cases inside window Z

\(E_Z\) = expected cases inside Z (proportional to population)

\(C\) = total cases in the study area

The test statistic is \(T = \max_Z \, \text{LLR}(Z)\)—the window with the highest LLR is the most likely cluster.
Inference via Monte Carlo simulation:

Generate k = 999 (or 9,999) datasets by randomly redistributing cases proportional to population
Compute T for each simulated dataset
\(p\text{-value} = \frac{\text{rank of observed } T \text{ among all } k+1 \text{ values}}{k+1}\)







Tip



Why Monte Carlo? SaTScan tests thousands of windows simultaneously. Monte Carlo simulation naturally accounts for this multiple-testing problem—no Bonferroni correction needed.

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
5 SaTScan Software: Input Files
SaTScan requires three plain-text files. Location IDs must match across all files.

5.1 Case file (.cas)
location_id   case_count   year [month day]
34005    12    2020
34007     8    2020
34009     3    2020
34013    21    2020


5.2 Population file (.pop)
location_id   population   year
34005    450000    2020
34007    280000    2020
34009    120000    2020
34013    510000    2020


5.3 Coordinates file (.geo)
location_id   latitude   longitude
34005    40.234    -74.678
34007    40.512    -74.321
34009    40.789    -74.123
34013    40.102    -74.891






Warning



Common error: Location IDs must be identical across all three files. A mismatch causes SaTScan to drop records silently.

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
6 SaTScan Software: Step-by-Step Walkthrough

🖥️ Live demo opportunity — walk through the GUI while narrating these steps.


6.1 Step 1 — New Session
File → New Session
Choose:

Analysis type: Purely Spatial

Probability model: Poisson



6.2 Step 2 — Input tab

Load Case File, Population File, Coordinates File

Set Time Precision (None for purely spatial; Year/Month/Day for temporal)

Set Study Period dates



6.3 Step 3 — Analysis tab

Max spatial cluster size: 50% of population at risk (default). Try 25% for sensitivity.

Cluster reporting: Gini coefficient or report up to N secondary clusters

High/Low rates: High rates only for most disease surveillance



6.4 Step 4 — Output tab

Set output file path (.txt for text report)

Enable optional outputs:

✅ Google Earth (.kml) — visualize in Google Earth instantly

✅ ArcGIS (.shp) — import cluster polygons into QGIS/ArcGIS

✅ Cluster Information — full details for every significant cluster




6.5 Step 5 — Spatial Window tab

Default: Circular

Switch to Elliptic for geographically elongated regions (river corridors, highway corridors)



6.6 Step 6 — Run
Click Run. Open the .txt output file. Results list:

Most Likely Cluster — highest LLR

Secondary Clusters — next highest LLR clusters that don’t overlap the most likely cluster

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
7 Reading SaTScan Output
A typical SaTScan text output section looks like this:
MOST LIKELY CLUSTER
-------------------
1. Location IDs included: 34005 34007 34013 34015
   Coordinates / radius:  (40.38 N, 74.51 W) / 18.3 km
   Population:            1,240,000
   Cases:                 87
   Expected cases:        43.2
   Annual cases / 100,000: 14.3
   Observed / expected:   2.01
   Log likelihood ratio:  27.58
   P-value:               0.001

SECONDARY CLUSTERS
------------------
2. ...

7.1 Key metrics explained







Metric
Meaning




Center & Radius
Geographic center and size of the cluster window


Observed (O)
Actual case count inside the window


Expected (E)
Cases expected under the null (proportional to pop.)


O / E
Relative Risk — how many times higher than background


LLR
Log-likelihood ratio; larger = stronger cluster signal


P-value
Proportion of MC simulations with T ≥ observed T









Tip



Rule of thumb: O/E > 1.5 with p < 0.05 is commonly used as a threshold for further investigation, but context always matters.

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
8 R Implementation: SpatialEpi Package
The SpatialEpi package provides a pure-R implementation via kulldorff() — no external executable required.

8.1 Setup and data


Code
# Install if needed:
# install.packages(c("SpatialEpi", "sf", "tmap", "dplyr"))

library(SpatialEpi)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(dplyr)

# Load the NY leukemia dataset (ships with SpatialEpi)
data(NYleukemia)

# Examine structure
glimpse(NYleukemia$data)


Rows: 281
Columns: 3
$ censustract.FIPS <fct> 36007000100, 36007000200, 36007000300, 36007000400, 3…
$ cases            <dbl> 3.08284, 4.08331, 1.08750, 1.06515, 3.06017, 1.06386,…
$ population       <dbl> 3540, 3560, 3739, 2784, 2571, 2729, 3952, 993, 1908, …




Code
# Geographic coordinates of census tract centroids
head(NYleukemia$geo)


  censustract.FIPS         x        y
1      36007000100 -75.94087 42.10782
2      36007000200 -75.93118 42.11099
3      36007000300 -75.92011 42.11738
4      36007000400 -75.89749 42.11801
5      36007000500 -75.90269 42.10872
6      36007000600 -75.88943 42.11400


Code
# Case and population data
head(NYleukemia$data)


  censustract.FIPS   cases population
1      36007000100 3.08284       3540
2      36007000200 4.08331       3560
3      36007000300 1.08750       3739
4      36007000400 1.06515       2784
5      36007000500 3.06017       2571
6      36007000600 1.06386       2729




8.2 Compute expected counts


Code
# Expected cases under null hypothesis (population-proportional)
pop      <- NYleukemia$data$population
cases    <- NYleukemia$data$cases

expected <- expected(population = pop,
                     cases      = cases,
                     n.strata   = 1)

# Quick sanity check: sum(expected) should equal sum(cases)
cat("Total observed cases:", sum(cases), "\n")


Total observed cases: 591.9998 


Code
cat("Total expected cases:", round(sum(expected), 1), "\n")


Total expected cases: 592 




8.3 Run the Kulldorff scan


Code
# NYleukemia$geo columns: (FIPS, longitude, latitude) — use positions 2:3
# latlong2grid() expects a data.frame with (longitude, latitude) as cols 1 and 2
geo <- latlong2grid(NYleukemia$geo[, 2:3])

# Merge the 4 surrounded tracts into their surrounding tracts
# (standard pre-processing per SpatialEpi documentation)
remove_tracts <- NYleukemia$surrounded
add_tracts    <- NYleukemia$surrounding

pop_adj   <- pop
cases_adj <- cases
pop_adj[add_tracts]   <- pop_adj[add_tracts]   + pop_adj[remove_tracts]
cases_adj[add_tracts] <- cases_adj[add_tracts] + cases_adj[remove_tracts]
pop_adj   <- pop_adj[-remove_tracts]
cases_adj <- cases_adj[-remove_tracts]
geo_adj   <- geo[-remove_tracts, ]

expected_adj <- expected(population = pop_adj, cases = cases_adj, n.strata = 1)

# Run spatial scan statistic
# pop.upper.bound = 0.5 means maximum cluster = 50% of population
set.seed(42)
result <- kulldorff(
  geo              = geo_adj,
  cases            = cases_adj,
  population       = pop_adj,
  expected.cases   = expected_adj,
  pop.upper.bound  = 0.5,
  n.simulations    = 999,
  alpha.level      = 0.05,
  plot             = FALSE
)




8.4 Inspect results


Code
# Most likely cluster
mlc <- result$most.likely.cluster
cat("Most Likely Cluster\n")


Most Likely Cluster


Code
cat("-------------------\n")


-------------------


Code
cat("Number of tracts:", length(mlc$location.IDs.included), "\n")


Number of tracts: 30 


Code
cat("Observed cases:", sum(cases_adj[mlc$location.IDs.included]), "\n")


Observed cases: 108.7639 


Code
cat("Expected cases:", round(mlc$expected.cases, 2), "\n")


Expected cases: 66.1 


Code
cat("O/E ratio (Relative Risk):", round(mlc$SMR, 2), "\n")


O/E ratio (Relative Risk): 1.65 


Code
cat("Log-likelihood ratio:", round(mlc$log.likelihood.ratio, 3), "\n")


Log-likelihood ratio: 13.282 


Code
cat("P-value:", mlc$p.value, "\n")


P-value: 0.001 


Code
# Secondary clusters
cat("\nSecondary clusters found:", length(result$secondary.clusters), "\n")



Secondary clusters found: 1 


Code
if (length(result$secondary.clusters) > 0) {
  sc <- result$secondary.clusters[[1]]
  cat("  Cluster 2 — LLR:", round(sc$log.likelihood.ratio, 3),
      " | p =", sc$p.value,
      " | O/E =", round(sc$SMR, 2), "\n")
}


  Cluster 2 — LLR: 8.5  | p = 0.028  | O/E = 1.95 




8.5 Map the clusters


Code
library(sp)

# Build adjusted SpatialPolygons — remove the 4 surrounded tracts to match kulldorff run
sp_adj <- SpatialPolygons(
  NYleukemia$spatial.polygon@polygons[-remove_tracts],
  proj4string = CRS("+proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84")
)

# Convert to sf and attach attributes
ny_sf <- st_as_sf(sp_adj)
ny_sf$cases    <- cases_adj
ny_sf$pop      <- pop_adj
ny_sf$expected <- expected_adj
ny_sf$SMR      <- cases_adj / expected_adj

# Flag cluster membership
ny_sf$cluster_status <- "Background"
ny_sf$cluster_status[mlc$location.IDs.included] <- "Most Likely Cluster"
if (length(result$secondary.clusters) > 0) {
  ny_sf$cluster_status[
    result$secondary.clusters[[1]]$location.IDs.included] <- "Secondary Cluster"
}
ny_sf$cluster_status <- factor(ny_sf$cluster_status,
  levels = c("Most Likely Cluster", "Secondary Cluster", "Background"))

# Map 1: SMR choropleth
p_smr <- ggplot(ny_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = SMR), color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "#F7F7F7", high = "#D6604D",
                       midpoint = 1, name = "SMR\n(O/E)") +
  labs(title = "Standardized Morbidity Ratio",
       subtitle = "NY Childhood Leukemia 1978–1982") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1A3A5C"))

# Map 2: cluster detection results
cluster_colors <- c("Most Likely Cluster" = "#F0A500",
                    "Secondary Cluster"   = "#1B7A8A",
                    "Background"          = "#E8EDF2")

p_cluster <- ggplot(ny_sf) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cluster_status), color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = ny_sf[ny_sf$cluster_status != "Background", ],
          fill = NA, color = "#1A3A5C", linewidth = .5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colors, name = "Cluster\nStatus") +
  labs(title = "SaTScan Cluster Detection",
       subtitle = paste0("Most Likely Cluster: O/E = ",
                         round(mlc$SMR, 2), ", p = ", mlc$p.value)) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1A3A5C"))

library(patchwork)
p_smr + p_cluster





NY Leukemia: most likely cluster (orange fill) identified by Kulldorff spatial scan.

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
9 R Implementation: rsatscan Package
For larger datasets or when you need SaTScan’s full feature set, rsatscan calls the SaTScan executable from R, giving you a fully reproducible workflow.


Code
# Requires SaTScan installed and rsatscan package
# install.packages("rsatscan")
library(rsatscan)

# ── 1. Reset options and write parameter file ──
ss.options(reset = TRUE)

# ── 2. Configure analysis parameters ──
ss.options(list(
  CaseFile              = "cases.cas",
  PopulationFile        = "pop.pop",
  CoordinatesFile       = "geo.geo",
  CoordinatesType       = 1,   # 1 = lat/lon
  AnalysisType          = 1,   # 1 = Purely Spatial
  ModelType             = 0,   # 0 = Poisson
  ScanAreas             = 1,   # 1 = High rates
  TimeAggregationUnits  = 3,   # 3 = Year
  MaxSpatialSizeInPopulationAtRisk = 50,
  MonteCarloReps        = 999,
  ResultsFile           = "output.txt",
  OutputShapefiles      = "y",          # Write .shp files
  OutputGoogleEarthKML  = "y"           # Write .kml file
))

# ── 3. Write input files from R data frames ──
write.cas(casefile,  tempdir(), "cases")
write.pop(popfile,   tempdir(), "pop")
write.geo(geofile,   tempdir(), "geo")

# ── 4. Run SaTScan ──
result <- satscan(
  prmlocation = tempdir(),
  prmfilename = "analysis",
  sslocation  = "/path/to/SaTScan"  # path to SaTScan executable
)

# ── 5. Examine results ──
summary(result)
result$col         # cluster information data frame
result$geo         # cluster geometry for mapping








Note



Tip: rsatscan returns results as R data frames, making it easy to pipe cluster results directly into ggplot2 or tmap for publication-quality maps. Set sslocation to wherever SaTScan is installed on your machine (e.g., "C:/Program Files/SaTScan" on Windows).

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
10 Space-Time Analysis: Detecting Outbreaks
For outbreak detection, use the Space-Time Permutation model (no population denominator needed).


Code
# Space-Time Permutation in rsatscan
ss.options(list(
  AnalysisType          = 3,   # 3 = Space-Time
  ModelType             = 2,   # 2 = Space-Time Permutation
  TimeAggregationUnits  = 2,   # 2 = Month
  TimeAggregationLength = 1,
  MaxTemporalSize       = 50,  # Max cluster spans 50% of study period
  MaxSpatialSizeInPopulationAtRisk = 25
))



10.1 What to look for in space-time output
MOST LIKELY CLUSTER
Coordinates:  (39.95 N, 75.17 W) / 3.2 km
Time frame:   2023/3 to 2023/5  (3 months)
Cases:        47    Expected: 12.4
O/E:          3.79
P-value:      0.001
A tight geographic radius plus a short time window = strong outbreak signal.

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
11 Assumptions, Limitations & Pitfalls


Code
library(ggplot2)

# Show circular window vs. irregular true cluster
set.seed(99)
# True elongated cluster (along a river/road)
true_cluster <- data.frame(
  x = c(rnorm(40, mean = seq(2, 7, length.out = 40), sd = 0.4)),
  y = c(rnorm(40, mean = seq(3, 3.8, length.out = 40), sd = 0.25))
)
background <- data.frame(
  x = runif(80, 0, 10), y = runif(80, 0, 7)
)

# Fitted circular window (best fit circle — will miss edges)
cx <- mean(true_cluster$x); cy <- mean(true_cluster$y)
r  <- 2.6

circle_fit <- data.frame(
  x = cx + r * cos(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 200)),
  y = cy + r * sin(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 200))
)

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = background, aes(x, y), color = "#A0ADB8", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(data = true_cluster, aes(x, y), color = "#1A3A5C", size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_path(data = circle_fit, aes(x, y), color = "#F0A500",
            linewidth = 1.3, linetype = "dashed") +
  annotate("label", x = cx, y = cy + r + 0.5,
           label = "Circular window (SaTScan default)",
           color = "#F0A500", size = 3.5, fill = "white") +
  annotate("label", x = 5.5, y = 4.2,
           label = "True elongated cluster\n(e.g., along a waterway)",
           color = "#1A3A5C", size = 3.5, fill = "white") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 7)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  labs(title = "Limitation: Circular Window Assumption",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#1A3A5C"),
        axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_line(color = "grey94"))





Circular windows may poorly represent elongated or irregular true cluster shapes.





11.1 Key limitations to discuss with students








Issue
Description
Mitigation




Circular windows
Real clusters are rarely circular
Use elliptic scan or FleXScan


Max cluster size
50% default may catch multi-cluster noise
Sensitivity analysis at 25%, 50%


Edge effects
Boundary clusters are truncated
Add buffer zone around study area


No covariates
Cannot adjust for age, SES, race
Stratify or use Bayesian alternatives


Population data
Poisson model needs accurate denominator
Use most recent ACS; interpolate if needed


Ecological fallacy
Area-level ≠ individual-level inference
Be explicit: clusters guide investigation, not causation


Reporting bias
Significant clusters tend to get published
Report all results; pre-register analyses









Warning



Critical point: A statistically significant SaTScan cluster is evidence of geographic concentration of disease — it is not proof of cause. Clusters always require follow-up with exposure data, contextual knowledge, and epidemiologic investigation.

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
12 SaTScan vs. Other Methods









Method
Core Approach
Strengths
Limitations




SaTScan
Moving circular window + LLR
Formal inference, p-values, free software
Circular window; no covariate adjustment


Local Moran’s I (LISA)
Local spatial autocorrelation
Exploratory; identifies hot/cold spots
No formal cluster test; sensitive to scale


Getis-Ord Gi*
Z-score of local weighted mean
Continuous surface; detects high-value areas
Assumes spatial stationarity


Knox Test
Space-time proximity pairs
Outbreak investigation
Requires threshold parameters


KDE
Smoothed density surface
Visual and intuitive
Subjective bandwidth; no inference


Bayesian (BYM)
Hierarchical spatial model
Smooths small-area rates; covariate adjustment
Complex MCMC; harder to explain

Final output: SMR and cluster detection side by side for the NY leukemia dataset.




Interpretation of these results:

The most likely cluster contains census tracts with O/E = 1.65, meaning approximately 65% more childhood leukemia cases than expected.
The p-value is 0.001, suggesting this cluster is unlikely to arise by chance under the null hypothesis of spatial randomness.
This cluster (Binghamton, NY area) prompted further investigation into proximity to nuclear power facilities and industrial waste sites — though causation requires additional study.

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
text:
14 Quick Reference: Common Workflow


Code
# ─── Complete workflow: SpatialEpi::kulldorff() ───────────────────────────

library(SpatialEpi)

# 1. Load / prepare data
#    geo    = data.frame with lat and lon (one row per area)
#    cases  = integer vector (cases per area)
#    pop    = integer vector (population per area)

# 2. Compute expected
expected <- expected(population = pop, cases = cases, n.strata = 1)

# 3. Convert coordinates
# latlong2grid() expects 2-column data.frame: (longitude, latitude)
# For NYleukemia: latlong2grid(NYleukemia$geo[, 2:3])
geo_grid <- latlong2grid(geo[, c("longitude", "latitude")])

# 4. Run scan
result <- kulldorff(
  geo              = geo_grid,
  cases            = cases,
  population       = pop,
  expected.cases   = expected,
  pop.upper.bound  = 0.50,       # max 50% of population
  n.simulations    = 999,
  alpha.level      = 0.05,
  plot             = FALSE
)

# 5. Extract results
result$most.likely.cluster$SMR              # Relative Risk
result$most.likely.cluster$p.value          # P-value
result$most.likely.cluster$location.IDs.included  # Which areas?

# 6. Map
# Flag cluster IDs in your sf object and use ggplot2 / tmap

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan

15 Summary






NoteKey Take-Aways




SaTScan uses a circular scanning window and a log-likelihood ratio test, with p-values from Monte Carlo simulation.
Three input files are required: case counts, population, and geographic coordinates — all as plain text with matching location IDs.
Choose your model: Poisson for counts with a denominator; Bernoulli for case-control; Space-Time Permutation when no population data is available.
In R, use SpatialEpi::kulldorff() for a self-contained analysis, or rsatscan to call the full SaTScan executable programmatically.
Interpret carefully: O/E gives relative risk; p-value tests against spatial randomness. A significant cluster is the start of an investigation, not a conclusion.
Know the limits: circular windows, no covariate adjustment, ecological inference only.

title: Spatial Cluster Detection with SaTScan
